ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The successful lunar landing and return of Chang'e-5 is inspiring. Xiaoming, knowing that there is no air on the Moon and thus no way to decelerate using parachutes, has designed a new type of landing device. This device consists of a cabin, parallel rails with a separation of $I$, a magnet producing a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B$ perpendicular to the plane of the cabin rails, and a ∧-shaped rigid wire frame. The side ab of the ∧-shaped wire frame can slide along the rails while maintaining good contact. The cabin, rails, and magnet are fixed together, with a total mass of $m_{1}$. The entire device has a velocity of magnitude $v_{0}$ immediately before landing vertically on the lunar surface. The velocity of the wire frame becomes zero immediately after making contact with the lunar surface. After deceleration, the cabin can be considered to be moving at a constant speed before the buffer spring below the rails contacts the lunar surface. It is given that the resistance of the cabin is 3r, the mass of the ∧-shaped wire frame is $m_{2}$, each of its 7 sides has a length of l, and each has a resistance of r. The gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface is $\frac{g}{6}$. Throughout the entire motion, only the side ab is in the magnetic field, the wire frame is insulated from the lunar surface, and the resistance and frictional resistance of the rails are neglected.

1. Determine the induced electromotive force $E$ generated in the side ab of the wire frame immediately after the landing device contacts the lunar surface.
2. Determine the current $I_{0}$ flowing through the ab-type wire frame immediately after the landing device contacts the lunar surface.
3. Determine the magnitude of the velocity $v$ of the cabin when it moves at a constant speed.
4. Xiaozhang, a classmate, believes that by connecting a capacitor with a capacitance of C between the two rails above the magnetic field, some energy can be recovered during the landing deceleration process. Under the condition that all other conditions remain unchanged, determine the magnitude of the velocity $v^{\prime}$ of the cabin when it moves at a constant speed.
5. The charge $q$ on the capacitor at this time.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there is an upper cabin (cabin), and two vertical guide rail (guide rails) are fixed below the cabin, with the spacing between the guide rails labeled l in the figure; in the guide-rail region there is a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the plane of the device. Below there is a ∧-shaped rigid wireframe (labeled 'A' wireframe in the figure), and the ab side at the upper end of the wireframe is respectively in contact with the two guide rails and can slide along the guide rails; in the figure, only the ab side is located in the magnetic-field region. Reasoning: Just after contacting the lunar surface, the velocity of the ∧-shaped wireframe immediately becomes 0, while the cabin, guide rails, and magnet still move at velocity v0 relative to the ab side, so the relative velocity with which the ab side cuts the magnetic induction lines is v0. According to the motional electromotive force formula, E0 = B l v0. Treating it according to the equivalent circuit of the structure given in the problem, the resistance of the ab side itself is r, and after the remaining ∧-shaped wireframe part and the cabin branch are equivalently treated, the total resistance corresponding to the ab current is 2r, so the current at the moment of just contacting is I0 = E0/(2r) = B l v0/(2r). When the cabin later falls at constant velocity v, similarly E = B l v, and the current I = B l v/(2r). At constant velocity, the forces on the cabin are balanced, the lunar-surface gravity is m1 g/6, and the magnitude of the upward magnetic damping force is B I l, so B l · B l v/(2r) = m1 g/6, solving gives v = m1 g r/(3 B^2 l^2). If a capacitor C is connected between the two guide rails above the magnetic field, after reaching constant velocity there is no steady current in the capacitor branch, so the steady-state current and terminal velocity do not change, v' = v = m1 g r/(3 B^2 l^2). At this time, the voltage across the capacitor equals the terminal voltage between the guide rails. From the voltage relation U = E - I r = E/2. Substituting E = B l v' at constant velocity gives U = m1 g r/(6 B l), so the capacitor charge q = C U = m1 g r C/(6 B l).
